missing_spec_content.spec_text: explain how the concept of an electric field helps to explain the non-contact force between charged objects as well as other electrostatic phenomena such as sparking.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson uses the electric field to explain the non-contact force: "Any other charged object placed in this field feels a force. The objects do not need to touch." It never uses the field to explain sparking. Sparks appear only as events ("a huge spark jumps between the cloud and the ground", "discharge as a spark"). The lesson does not explain that a strong electric field near a highly charged object can ionise the air and let charge jump across as a spark. The only nearby idea is in the Lightning key term, which talks about potential difference ionising the air. It does not link this to the electric field.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: draw the electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives only the direction of the lines: "Around an isolated positive charge, field lines point outward" and "Positive charge: field lines radiate outward". There is no diagram (diagram is null). The lesson never says the lines are straight, radial, evenly spread and at right angles to the surface of the sphere, so the student is not taught how to draw the pattern for a sphere.

above_gcse.text: Between two parallel plates with opposite charges, the field is uniform. The field lines are parallel, equally spaced and at right angles to the plates.
above_gcse.why: The specification asks only for the field pattern of an isolated charged sphere. Uniform fields between parallel plates are not in these sections. The same content is repeated in writeBullets, keyTerms ("Uniform electric field"), examTips[1], revisionCardBullets[7] and tutor_note.

above_gcse.text: Inkjet printers: ink droplets are given a charge. Electric field plates deflect the charged droplets so they hit exact spots on the paper.
above_gcse.why: The specification sections do not list any applications of static electricity. Inkjet printers, photocopiers/laser printers, electrostatic precipitators and electrostatic paint spraying are all beyond these sections. They take up a whole key point, a table, a checkpoint and several revision bullets.

above_gcse.text: Drum is charged by corona wire; laser removes charge selectively
above_gcse.why: Corona wires and the details of the photocopier drum are well beyond the specification.

above_gcse.text: Oppositely charged plates attract particles; they fall into collection hoppers
above_gcse.why: Precipitator engineering details (high-voltage wire, collection hoppers, "up to 99% of particles") are not required by the specification.

above_gcse.text: Aircraft build up static charge in flight, from friction with the air. Bonding cables connect the aircraft and the fuelling vehicle.
above_gcse.why: Bonding cables, earthing of tankers and aircraft refuelling procedures are not in these specification sections. The spec asks only that sparking be described and explained.

above_gcse.text: Ice crystals and water droplets collide and transfer charge. This makes the base of the cloud negatively charged.
above_gcse.why: The mechanism of charge separation in storm clouds is not required by the specification.

above_gcse.text: occurs when potential difference becomes large enough to ionise the air
above_gcse.why: Ionisation of air by potential difference is not mentioned in these sections. It is not linked to the electric field ideas the spec does require, so it could confuse.

factual_errors.text: Charge is conserved: the amount of negative charge gained equals the positive charge lost.
factual_errors.correction: One material gains negative charge (electrons). The other loses those electrons and is left with an equal positive charge. No positive charge is "lost". The spec says: "The material that loses electrons is left with an equal positive charge."

factual_errors.text: Static electricity only builds up on insulators. Conductors let charge flow away.
factual_errors.correction: A conductor can hold static charge if it is insulated from the ground. Examples are a person in rubber-soled shoes, a Van de Graaff dome, a fuel tanker or an aircraft. The lesson itself says metal tankers and aircraft build up charge, which contradicts this statement. Conductors lose their charge only when connected to earth.

factual_errors.text: In both cases, charge builds up on an insulating surface until it suddenly discharges.
factual_errors.correction: In the carpet and door-handle shock, the charge builds up on your body. Your body is a conductor, insulated from the ground by your shoes. In lightning, the charge is in the cloud. Neither case is simply "an insulating surface".

factual_errors.text: The car body is earthed (opposite charge), so it attracts all the droplets.
factual_errors.correction: Earthing does not give the car body an opposite charge. An earthed body stays at zero potential, and an opposite charge is induced on it as the charged droplets approach. Some systems give the body an opposite charge directly. Treating "earthed" and "opposite charge" as the same thing is wrong. The same error appears in checkpoints[3].wrongFeedback: "The car body (earthed, opposite charge) then attracts them all."

factual_errors.text: Photocopiers (laser printers): a drum is charged. Laser light removes charge from areas that should stay white.
factual_errors.correction: Photocopiers and laser printers are different devices. In a traditional photocopier, light reflected from the white parts of the original (usually not a laser) discharges the drum. In a laser printer, the laser usually discharges the areas where toner should go, and toner of the same charge sticks to those discharged areas. The lesson's single description is correct for neither device as stated.

wrong_terms.text: Around an isolated positive charge, field lines point outward.
Unlike (opposite) charges attract each other. Like (same) charges repel each other.
wrong_terms.spec_term: Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel. Two objects that carry different types of charge attract.

checkpoint_mismatch.why: Checkpoint 2 asks why fuel tanker lorries are earthed. That content comes from keyPoints[3] (Dangers and uses), not from the Electric fields key point it sits with. Nothing in keyPoints[2] supports the answer, and no checkpoint tests electric fields at all.

not_checked: All keyPoints have "diagram": null, so there were no diagrams of field patterns to check. Whether the lesson supports the spec skill 'draw the electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere' could only be judged from the text.
The spec lists 'Key opportunities for skills development WS 1.2, 1.5'. The text of these working-scientifically statements was not provided, so coverage could not be checked.
